title: The raft
hookLine: the Buddha: a raft is for crossing, not for carrying on your head afterward (Majjhima Nikaya 22)

lines: WHEN A METHOD HAS DONE ITS JOB.
cards: What do you do with a useful thing once it's done its job? Every path has its methods: ways of praying, sitting, learning. And this has been a week of many houses.
Mencius and the child at the well. Confucius watching the river. Satyakama's plain truth.
Guru Nanak's honest bread, and his feet toward the Kaaba. A father running down a road. Chinese, Hindu, Sikh and Christian stories, each from its own home.
The week ends with the Buddha, and his answer to that odd question.

teach.b: The Buddha is speaking to his monks, in the twenty-second discourse of the Middle Length collection. Suppose, he says, a man on a long journey comes to a wide river.
The near bank is dangerous and frightening; the far bank is safe. No ferry, no bridge.
So he gathers grass, sticks, branches and leaves, ties them into a raft, and paddling with his hands and feet, he makes it across. On the safe side, he thinks: this raft was so useful to me.
I should pick it up and carry it on my head wherever I go. Would that man be doing the right thing with the raft? the Buddha asks. No, say the monks.
He should pull it up on the shore, or leave it floating, and go on his way.
Then the startling part: in the same way, the Buddha says, the teaching itself is like a raft. It's for crossing over, not for holding onto. He's talking about his own teaching.
Buddhist teachers read that letting go in more than one way.
It doesn't mean the teaching is useless; the whole story says how useful the raft was. It means don't cling to it, don't turn it into something to own and defend. Use it to cross.
Ordinary life has rafts too: the training wheels, the flashcards, the alarm you needed for years and then didn't. There's no shame in how much you needed a raft.
The only mistake is carrying it on your head after you've reached the shore.

how: Buddhist teachers use the simile of the raft to explain that the teachings are tools for liberation rather than possessions to cling to or argue over.

o: a vow to hold your teacher's words forever
a lifeboat kept only for the most devoted
a teaching used to cross over, then set down

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the Buddha says the raft was useless
it carried the man across. the point is not to cling to it afterward.
the Buddha applies the raft to his own teaching
the teaching is for crossing over, not for holding onto.
the man should carry the raft on his head
he should pull it ashore or leave it floating, and go on.

games.q: you've crossed the river on a raft you built. you're safe on the far bank. what do you do with the raft?
o: carry it on your head, in gratitude
leave it on the shore and go on
burn it so no one else can use it
games.why: leave it: pull it ashore or let it float, and go on. the Buddha says his own teaching is like that raft, for crossing, not for holding.

practice: Think of the habits, rules and tricks that get you through a day, and find one you still carry after it stopped helping: a way of working that fit an old job, a rule from a hard season that's over now.
Thank it honestly; it got you across something. Then picture setting it down on the bank, gently, and walking on a few steps without it.

wordCard.voice: The raft. The Buddha's picture of a teaching as something for crossing over, useful, and then set down on the far shore.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: kulla, a raft. the simile of the raft is the kullupama.

carryVoice: Your line: leave the raft. Useful once doesn't mean carried around forever. Day eighty-four, done.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (the simile of the raft)
